name: Wellbeing, Behavior, Attendance, and Safety
blurb: A study of 14 companies that monitor students online found that most watch students around the clock, not just during school hours. Most use AI to flag concerning content, but fewer than half described any human review of those flags.
title: Wellbeing, Behavior, Attendance, and Safety
answer: A study of 14 companies that monitor students online found that most watch students around the clock, not just during school hours. Most use AI to flag concerning content, but fewer than half described any human review of those flags.

papers.title: What Works to Keep Students in School? A Meta-Analysis of Interventions to Reduce School Absenteeism
papers.caveat: Pooled effects hide variation across settings.
papers.finding: Meta-analysis of 13 studies (2020 to 2025): small effect, g = 0.091; stronger in single-school implementations.

papers.title: Lifting Up Attendance in Rural Districts: A Multi-Site Trial of a Personalized Messaging Campaign
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in 47 rural districts, 16 states: absences down 1.7% to 4.5% at about $4 per student; 0.2 to 0.5 days saved.

papers.title: Effectiveness of AI-Driven Conversational Agents in Improving Mental Health Among Young People: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.caveat: Pooled effects hide variation across settings.
papers.finding: Meta-analysis, 15 RCTs, ages 12 to 25: g = 0.61 for depressive symptoms; no effect on anxiety, stress, or wellbeing after bias adjustment.

papers.title: School-Based Online Surveillance of Youth: Systematic Search and Content Analysis of Surveillance Company Websites
papers.finding: 14 school monitoring companies: 86% monitor 24/7 outside school, 71% use AI flagging, fewer than half have human review, 2 contact police at their discretion.

papers.title: Can Personalized Attendance Information Mitigate Student Absenteeism? Evidence from Six Randomized Field Trials
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: Six district-run RCTs, 78,000 PreK to 12 students: personalized parent messages cut absences 1.9%.

papers.title: The Effectiveness of AI Chatbots in Alleviating Mental Distress and Promoting Health Behaviors Among Adolescents and Young Adults
papers.caveat: Pooled effects hide variation across settings.
papers.finding: 31 RCTs: small to moderate reduction in distress (SMD -0.35); scripted systems consistent, generative systems inconclusive.

papers.title: Current Landscape and Future Directions for Mental Health Conversational Agents for Youth: Scoping Review
papers.finding: 39 youth mental health chatbots: limited safety features for imminent risk; 90% of studies ignored ethics.

papers.title: Use of automated conversational agents in improving young population mental health: a scoping review
papers.finding: 25 studies: youth chatbots are acceptable and usable, but almost half of evaluations found no effect on emotional outcomes.

papers.title: Investigating Advanced School Surveillance Practices and Disproportionality: A Systematic Review
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: 31 studies: surveillance technology concentrates in schools serving poor and minoritized students; mixed effects on perceived safety.

papers.why: Names concrete social media stressors counselors and digital citizenship lessons can address.
papers.title: The effects of personality and social media experiences on mental health: Examining the mediating role of fear of missing out, ghosting, and vaguebooking
papers.finding: Online survey of 995 adolescents and young adults (mostly Europe). Fear of missing out, being ghosted, and vaguebooking formed a triad that mediated links between personality, social media use, and mental health.

papers.title: Attitudes Toward School-Based Surveillance of Adolescents' Social Media Activity
papers.finding: Survey of young adults, parents, teachers, administrators: young adults saw less benefit and more risk; nonheterosexual and minority respondents saw higher risk.

papers.why: Supports digital wellbeing and anti-cyberbullying ideas in the student support and digital citizenship chapters.
papers.title: Internet use and cyberbullying: Impacts on psychosocial and psychosomatic wellbeing among Chinese adolescents
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional, self-report, China; correlation not cause.
papers.finding: Survey of 3,378 middle school students (ages 11-16) in three Chinese provinces. Over 3 hours per day of entertainment internet use linked to more anxiety (OR 1.6), depression (OR 2.1), and physical complaints. Moderate gaming was not harmful. 37.5% reported cyberbullying involvement; bully-victims were most at risk.

papers.title: Using Chatbot Technology to Improve Brazilian Adolescents' Body Image and Mental Health at Scale
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, adolescents 13 to 18: small body image and affect gains; 62% attrition.

papers.title: Association of Online Risk Factors With Subsequent Youth Suicide-Related Behaviors in the US
papers.finding: Case-control study using monitoring vendor data from 2,600 schools: online risk signals were associated with later severe self-harm alerts. Association, not proof that monitoring prevents harm.

papers.title: Social Media Surveillance in Schools: Rethinking Public Health Interventions in the Digital Age
papers.finding: No evidence supports vendor claims that social media surveillance addresses student health or safety; may harm marginalized youth.

papers.title: Reducing Student Absenteeism in the Early Grades by Targeting Parental Beliefs
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in 10 districts, grades K to 5: parent mailings cut chronic absence 15%.

papers.title: Reducing student absences at scale by targeting parents' misbeliefs
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, parents of 28,080 high-risk K-12 students: personalized mailings on total absences cut chronic absence by 10% or more by correcting parents' underestimates.

children.name: Attendance and Early Warning
children.blurb: Attendance and early warning is a practice that uses attendance data and risk predictions to trigger a human response, not to label a student.

children.name: Why Students Miss School
children.blurb: Attendance data records how many days a student missed, not why.

children.name: Check Ins, Surveys, and Counselor Triage
children.blurb: Check ins, surveys, and counselor triage are ways for schools to hear how students are doing, spot patterns, and route urgent concerns to a trained adult quickly.

children.name: Anonymous Reports
children.blurb: Anonymous reporting tools give students a way to raise bullying, threats, or other concerns without exposing themselves to retaliation.

children.name: Crisis Language Goes to a Person
children.blurb: Crisis language goes to a person means that any student-facing tool for feelings or health must send signs of self harm, suicide, abuse, or danger to a trained adult immediately.

children.name: Self Help Tools for Mild Distress
children.blurb: Self help tools for mild distress are chatbots that use techniques such as cognitive behavioral therapy to help young people manage mild emotional distress.

children.name: Device Monitoring
children.blurb: Device monitoring is the practice of paying companies to scan what students do on school devices and accounts for signs of self harm, violence, or other risks.

children.name: Discipline and Behavior Data
children.blurb: Discipline data can reveal unfair patterns, where some groups of students are disciplined more often or more harshly than others for similar behavior.

children.name: Bullying, Cyberbullying, and Deepfakes
children.blurb: Bullying now often happens online, where adults cannot see it, and AI has added fake images and videos of real students as a new form of harm.

children.name: Students' Trust and Rights
children.blurb: Every safety, wellbeing and attendance tool described in this chapter only works if students trust the adults and systems around them.

children.name: Threat Assessment
children.blurb: Threat assessment is the process a school uses when a student may pose a danger to others, in which a trained team gathers information, judges how serious the concern is and decides on a response.

children.name: Health Office Patterns
children.blurb: The health office keeps a record of when students visit and why, and patterns across those visits can signal anxiety, bullying or an unmet health need.

children.name: Mentoring and Digital Wellbeing
children.blurb: Mentoring and digital wellbeing is the practice of pairing students with supportive adults while also teaching students how to manage their own screen habits and emotions.

children.name: Physical Safety and Security
children.blurb: Physical safety and security in a school covers who enters the building, how staff prepare for emergencies, and how sensitive data is protected from cyber threats.

sections.body: This part of school life is the work of noticing when a student is absent, in distress, in danger, or unsafe, and deciding what to do next. The book says AI can help spot signals, such as a student in crisis, a threat before violence, or a pattern of absence before a student drops out. It can also watch students around the clock without their knowledge, flag the wrong students, and send police to a child's home over a misread message. The chapter covers attendance and early warning, check ins and surveys, anonymous reports, wellness tools and crisis routing, self help chatbots, device monitoring, discipline and behavior data, threat assessment, health office patterns, and physical safety. Figure 15.2 maps the ideas and their evidence, and the book notes that only attendance outreach carries strong evidence while device monitoring has none showing it prevents harm.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works is attendance outreach, and the research held for this chapter includes What Works to Keep Students in School? A Meta-Analysis of Interventions to Reduce School Absenteeism, Lifting Up Attendance in Rural Districts, and Can Personalized Attendance Information Mitigate Student Absenteeism? as evidence that outreach and personalized messages can reduce absences. What does not work is trusting a tool to decide alone: device monitoring has no evidence showing it prevents harm, and Social Media Surveillance in Schools says no evidence supports vendor claims that social media surveillance addresses student health or safety and may harm marginalized youth. The rule the book holds to is that the system can flag, but a person must reach out, so every signal leads to a trained human who looks at the full picture and decides what to do. No machine should decide whether a student is safe, in danger, or dangerous, and the common failures are a flag that goes nowhere or a flag acted on without a person. The board question asks who reviews a flag, how quickly, and what they do, and the Thirty Day Move is to test crisis routing in every tool students can use to express feelings, map the chain from flag to person for every early warning, reporting, and monitoring tool, and review device monitoring against the conditions in Figure 15.5 before renewal.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: For attendance, a teacher or leader starts with Attendance and Early Warning and Why Students Miss School to see how signals and reasons connect, then uses the attendance research as evidence. For student voice and distress, Check Ins, Surveys, and Counselor Triage, Anonymous Reports, and Crisis Language Goes to a Person show how a flag should reach a trained person, while Self Help Tools for Mild Distress covers chatbots for lower level need. For monitoring and behavior, Device Monitoring, Discipline and Behavior Data, Bullying, Cyberbullying, and Deepfakes, and Students' Trust and Rights help leaders and parents weigh surveillance against rights and trust. For risk and safety, Threat Assessment, Health Office Patterns, Mentoring and Digital Wellbeing, and Physical Safety and Security connect the chain from flag to person across safety, health, and support. A parent would go to Students' Trust and Rights and Device Monitoring to understand what is watched, while a leader would use the board question and Thirty Day Move to check who reviews flags and how quickly.
